node-1.label: Patient presented with stridor, increased work of breathing, and supplemental oxygen requirement

node-2.label: Patient presented to the ED on transfer from an outside hospital after falling with an e-cigarette in his mouth several hours earlier; he did not remember the exact cause of the fall and believed he may have lost consciousness

node-3.label: Physical examination in the ED showed diffuse supraglottic edema most severe in the epiglottis, arytenoids, and aryepiglottic folds, which obstructed the view of the true vocal cords

why.why: CT confirms glottic and supraglottic swelling without fracture, and direct laryngoscopy shows diffuse edema with mucosal sloughing most severe in the epiglottis. The radiologist interprets this pattern as consistent with thermal/chemical injury from e-cigarette aspiration. Combined with the history of falling with an e-cigarette in his mouth, these findings strongly support e-cigarette airway injury, raising confidence from 0.65 to 0.85.

Although the supraglottic edema pattern is compatible with infectious supraglottitis, the trauma context and the radiologist's assessment that the mucosal sloughing pattern is most consistent with thermal/chemical injury make infection less likely. No new evidence supports an infectious cause, so confidence is lowered from 0.15 to 0.08.

Radiologist analysis reinforces a thermal/chemical injury pattern on CT and direct laryngoscopy. There remains no allergic trigger in the history and no new evidence for angioedema, so confidence is lowered from 0.05 to 0.02.

CT shows no laryngeal fracture, and direct laryngoscopy demonstrates diffuse mucosal sloughing most severe in the epiglottis, which is more consistent with thermal/chemical injury than local trauma. The radiologist explicitly states that traumatic injury is less likely given the absence of fracture, so confidence is lowered from 0.15 to 0.05.
